questions.q: What does PostgreSQL's $$ ... $$ dollar-quoting syntax solve?
options: It tells PostgreSQL to run the function asynchronously
It delimits a function's code body without needing to escape single quotes used inside it
It marks a variable as a global constant
It encrypts the function body in storage
questions.explain: Dollar-quoting avoids the need to escape literal single quotes inside the function body, which gets unreadable fast without it.

questions.q: Why does T-SQL never need an equivalent to dollar-quoting?
options: T-SQL automatically escapes all quotes for you
A T-SQL procedure body isn't a quoted string literal in the first place, so the escaping problem never arises
T-SQL doesn't allow string literals inside procedures
T-SQL procedures are always written in a separate file
questions.explain: The dollar-quoting problem is specific to how PostgreSQL treats a function body as a delimited string; T-SQL's batch syntax doesn't have this constraint.

questions.q: Why does PL/pgSQL's block structure resemble Oracle's PL/SQL more than it resembles T-SQL?
options: PostgreSQL's procedural language was deliberately modeled on Oracle's, using the same DECLARE/BEGIN/EXCEPTION/END structure
PL/pgSQL and T-SQL are actually identical, and PL/SQL is the odd one out
PostgreSQL copied its syntax from MySQL, not Oracle
There is no meaningful resemblance between any of the three
questions.explain: PL/pgSQL's formal block structure directly echoes the Oracle PL/SQL structure covered in Chapter 6, more than T-SQL's looser batch style.

questions.q: What PostgreSQL keyword introduces the primary way to define procedural logic, even for logic T-SQL would write as a stored procedure?
options: DEFINE ROUTINE ... AS plpgsql
CREATE FUNCTION ... LANGUAGE plpgsql
CREATE BLOCK ... LANGUAGE plpgsql
CREATE PROCEDURE ... LANGUAGE tsql
questions.explain: PostgreSQL leans on CREATE FUNCTION for almost everything procedural, even though it also has CREATE PROCEDURE for cases needing internal transaction control.

questions.q: How do you call a PL/pgSQL function like get_customer_total(42)?
options: CALL FUNCTION get_customer_total(42);
RUN get_customer_total(42);
SELECT get_customer_total(42); — called like any expression, inside a SELECT
EXEC get_customer_total 42;
questions.explain: Functions are called as expressions inside a SELECT, unlike T-SQL's EXEC for procedures.
